name: Biceps brachii
func: The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm. It bends the elbow and, most powerfully, turns the palm to face up, like turning a doorknob or screwdriver.

levels.kid:
Make a muscle with your arm, like a superhero! The bump that pops up on the front of your upper arm is your **biceps**.

When the biceps squeezes, it pulls your forearm up and **bends your elbow**. It also helps you **turn your hand** so your palm faces up, like when you hold out your hand for a cookie or turn a doorknob.

"Bi" means two, because the biceps has **two heads** at the top that join together. It works as a team with the triceps on the back of your arm.
levels.hs:
The **biceps brachii** ("two-headed muscle of the arm") lies on the front of the upper arm, just under the skin, over the deeper **brachialis** muscle.

It has two heads that start on the **scapula**. The **long head** starts on the **supraglenoid tubercle**, just above the shoulder socket, and its tendon runs inside the shoulder joint and down the **intertubercular (bicipital) groove** of the humerus. The **short head** starts on the **coracoid process**, a hook on the front of the scapula. The two bellies join and insert by a strong tendon on the **radial tuberosity** of the forearm, plus a flat sheet called the **bicipital aponeurosis**, which blends into the forearm fascia.

Its actions:
It **flexes the elbow**, especially when the palm is up.
It is the most powerful **supinator** of the forearm (turning the palm up).
It weakly helps flex the shoulder.

It is supplied by the **musculocutaneous nerve** (C5–C6). Tapping its tendon at the elbow produces the **biceps reflex**, which tests C5–C6. The tendon is easy to feel at the front of the elbow, with the **brachial artery** and median nerve just on its inner side.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** long head from the supraglenoid tubercle and the superior glenoid labrum; short head from the tip of the coracoid process (shared with coracobrachialis). Insertion: the posterior rough part of the **radial tuberosity**, plus the **bicipital aponeurosis** to the deep fascia over the medial forearm.

**Supination mechanics:** in pronation, the biceps tendon is wrapped around the radius. Contraction unwinds it, rotating the radius into supination. Supination is strongest with the elbow flexed to about 90°, which is why screws are designed for right-handed people to tighten clockwise. With the elbow straight, **supinator** does most of the work.

**Elbow flexion:** the biceps works with **brachialis** (the main, "workhorse" flexor regardless of forearm position) and **brachioradialis** (strongest in mid-pronation).

**Innervation and blood supply:** the **musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6)** pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis, continuing as the **lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm**. Blood comes from muscular branches of the **brachial artery**.

**Relations:** the **cubital fossa** contains, from lateral to medial, the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve ("TAN": tendon, artery, nerve). The bicipital aponeurosis passes over the brachial artery and median nerve, protecting them, while the **median cubital vein** lies superficial to the aponeurosis, a common site for blood draws.

**Long head tendon:** it is intra-articular but extrasynovial, held in the groove by the **transverse humeral ligament** and the rotator interval "pulley". It helps stabilise the humeral head.
levels.phd:
The biceps is a classic subject in muscle mechanics because it crosses two joints and has two heads with different roles. Its moment arm for supination is maximal near mid-range and drops near full supination, while its elbow flexion moment arm peaks near 90–100° of flexion. EMG shows the CNS uses the biceps preferentially when flexion and supination are both needed, and suppresses it when the task requires flexion in pronation, in which case brachialis dominates. This illustrates **task-dependent muscle selection** within a redundant system.

The long head's attachment to the **superior labrum** links it to shoulder pathology. The **biceps–labral complex** varies in how the tendon blends into the labrum (classified by Vangsness), and repetitive traction during throwing (especially the deceleration phase) or a "peel-back" mechanism in abduction and external rotation can detach the labrum, producing a **SLAP lesion** (superior labrum anterior to posterior).

Muscle architecture: the biceps has long, mostly parallel fascicles with a relatively low pennation angle, favouring range and speed. Fibre-type proportions are around 40–50% type I in untrained adults, but strength training mainly increases fibre cross-section (hypertrophy) with modest shifts in subtype.

Hypertrophy research uses the biceps heavily. Mechanical tension activates **mTORC1** signalling and increases muscle protein synthesis; **satellite cells** (Pax7-positive stem cells) fuse with fibres to add nuclei during sustained growth. The biceps reflex arc involves Ia afferents from muscle spindles synapsing monosynaptically on alpha motor neurons at C5–C6.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** test elbow flexion with the forearm supinated, and supination against resistance. The **biceps reflex** (C5–C6) is reduced in C5–C6 radiculopathy or a musculocutaneous nerve lesion and brisk with an upper motor neuron lesion.

**Distal biceps tendon rupture:** usually in middle-aged people lifting a heavy load with a flexed elbow (eccentric load). Signs: a pop at the elbow, bruising, a muscle belly that has retracted upward ("reverse Popeye"), and marked weakness in supination more than flexion. The **hook test** is key: the examiner cannot hook a finger under the tendon from the lateral side. MRI confirms. In active people, surgical reattachment to the radial tuberosity is usually recommended early, before the tendon retracts and scars.

**Proximal long head rupture:** often in older people with rotator cuff disease. The belly drops down, giving the **Popeye sign**. Function is usually only slightly reduced (the short head and brachialis compensate), so non-surgical care is common.

**Long head tendinopathy and SLAP tears** cause anterior shoulder pain. Tests include **Speed's test** (pain on resisted shoulder flexion with the elbow straight and palm up), **Yergason's test** (pain on resisted supination) and **O'Brien's test**. Treatments include rest, physiotherapy and, if needed, **tenodesis** or **tenotomy**.

**Musculocutaneous nerve injury** (rare, from penetrating trauma or shoulder surgery) weakens elbow flexion and supination and causes numbness on the lateral forearm.

In nerve transfer surgery for brachial plexus injuries, the **Oberlin transfer** uses an ulnar nerve fascicle to restore biceps function.

keyPoints: Two heads: long (supraglenoid tubercle) and short (coracoid)
Inserts on the radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis
Flexes the elbow; strongest supinator of the forearm
Musculocutaneous nerve C5–C6; biceps reflex C5–C6
Distal rupture → reverse Popeye; proximal → Popeye sign

test.q: What is the most powerful action of the biceps brachii?
test.explain: The biceps is the strongest supinator, especially with the elbow flexed.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the biceps brachii?
test.explain: It runs between biceps and brachialis and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

test.q: Where does the long head of biceps attach?
test.explain: The long head starts above the glenoid and runs through the shoulder joint.

test.q: Which test is positive when a distal biceps tendon is ruptured?
test.explain: The examiner cannot hook a finger under the absent tendon.

test.q: The biceps reflex tests which spinal levels?
test.explain: Tapping the biceps tendon tests mainly C5, with C6.
